claim: Behavior varies even among genetically identical animals raised in the same environment.
source: Behavior varies even among genetically identical animals raised in the same environment.
evidence: This is a general statement establishing the phenomenon of behavioral individuality, supported by the broader scientific literature and the context of the study.

claim: Little is known about the circuit or anatomical origins of behavioral individuality.
source: However, little is known about the circuit or anatomical origins of this individuality.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as of the study's publication.

claim: Idiosyncratic calcium responses in projection neuron dendrites correlate with individual preferences in a choice between two aversive odorants.
source: Namely, idiosyncratic calcium responses in projection neuron (PN) dendrites and densities of the presynaptic protein Bruchpilot in olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) axon terminals correlate with individual preferences in a choice between two aversive odorants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental calcium imaging data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Densities of the presynaptic protein Bruchpilot in olfactory receptor neuron axon terminals correlate with individual preferences in a choice between two aversive odorants.
source: Namely, idiosyncratic calcium responses in projection neuron (PN) dendrites and densities of the presynaptic protein Bruchpilot in olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) axon terminals correlate with individual preferences in a choice between two aversive odorants.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental Bruchpilot imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The ORN-PN synapse appears to be a locus of individuality where microscale variation gives rise to idiosyncratic behavior.
source: The ORN-PN synapse appears to be a locus of individuality where microscale variation gives rise to idiosyncratic behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined calcium imaging, Bruchpilot imaging, and modeling results.

claim: Simulating microscale stochasticity in ORN-PN synapses of a 3062 neuron model of the antennal lobe recapitulates patterns of variation in PN calcium responses matching experiments.
source: Simulating microscale stochasticity in ORN-PN synapses of a 3062 neuron model of the antennal lobe recapitulates patterns of variation in PN calcium responses matching experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling work presented in Figure 4.

claim: Stochasticity in other compartments of the antennal lobe circuit does not recapitulate patterns of PN calcium response variation seen in experiments.
source: Conversely, stochasticity in other compartments of this circuit does not recapitulate those patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling work presented in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: Individuality is observed across species including round worms, aphids, fish, mice, and people.
source: Such variability is observed across species, including round worms (Stern et al., 2017), aphids (Schuett et al., 2011), fish (Laskowski et al., 2022), mice (Freund et al., 2013), and people (Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies on behavioral individuality in various species.

claim: Flies exhibit individuality in many behaviors.
source: Flies exhibit individuality in many behaviors (Werkhoven et al., 2021), and the mechanistic origins of this variation have been studied for phototactic preference (Kain et al., 2012), temperature preference (Kain et al., 2015), locomotor handedness (Ayroles et al., 2015; Buchanan et al., 2015; de Bivort et al., 2022), object-fixated walking (Linneweber et al., 2020), and odor preference (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies on behavioral individuality in Drosophila.

claim: The neural substrates of individuality are poorly understood.
source: Generally, the neural substrates of individuality are poorly understood, though in a small number of instances nanoscale circuit correlates of individual behavioral biases have been identified (Lillvis et al., 2022; Linneweber et al., 2020; Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field, with citations to a few studies that have identified circuit correlates.

claim: The antennal lobe features approximately 50 anatomically identifiable microcircuits called glomeruli.
source: The AL features ~50 anatomically identifiable microcircuits called glomeruli (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the Drosophila olfactory system.

claim: Each glomerulus represents an odor-coding channel and receives axon inputs from olfactory receptor neurons expressing the same olfactory receptor gene.
source: Each glomerulus represents an odor-coding channel and receives axon inputs from olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) expressing the same olfactory receptor gene (de Bruyne et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the organization of the Drosophila olfactory system, supported by a citation.

claim: Uniglomerular projection neurons carry odor information from each glomerulus deeper into the brain.
source: Uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs) carry odor information from each glomerulus deeper into the brain (Jeanne and Wilson, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila olfactory system, supported by a citation.

claim: AL-intrinsic local neurons project among glomeruli and modulate odor representations.
source: AL-intrinsic local neurons (LNs) project among glomeruli (Chou et al., 2010) and modulate odor representations (Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila olfactory system, supported by citations.

claim: Individual flies differ in their PN calcium responses to identical odor stimuli.
source: Individual flies differ in their PN calcium responses to identical odor stimuli, as well as their odor-vs.-odor preference choices (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study and is also demonstrated in the current study's data.

claim: Individual flies differ in their odor-vs.-odor preference choices.
source: Individual flies differ in their PN calcium responses to identical odor stimuli, as well as their odor-vs.-odor preference choices (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study and is also demonstrated in the current study's data.

claim: The extent of preference variability depends on dopamine and serotonergic modulation.
source: The extent of preference variability depends on dopamine and serotonergic modulation (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The number of ORNs and PNs innervating a given glomerulus varies within hemispheres.
source: With respect to wiring variation, the number of ORNs and PNs innervating a given glomerulus varies within hemispheres (Tobin et al., 2017) and across individuals (Grabe et al., 2016; Schlegel et al., 2020), as does the glomerulus-innervation pattern of individual LNs (Chou et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The number of ORNs and PNs innervating a given glomerulus varies across individuals.
source: With respect to wiring variation, the number of ORNs and PNs innervating a given glomerulus varies within hemispheres (Tobin et al., 2017) and across individuals (Grabe et al., 2016; Schlegel et al., 2020), as does the glomerulus-innervation pattern of individual LNs (Chou et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The glomerulus-innervation pattern of individual LNs varies.
source: With respect to wiring variation, the number of ORNs and PNs innervating a given glomerulus varies within hemispheres (Tobin et al., 2017) and across individuals (Grabe et al., 2016; Schlegel et al., 2020), as does the glomerulus-innervation pattern of individual LNs (Chou et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Wiring asymmetry in an individual fly's dorsal cluster neurons is predictive of the straightness of its object-oriented walking behavior.
source: Wiring asymmetry in an individual fly's dorsal cluster neurons is predictive of the straightness of its object-oriented walking behavior (Linneweber et al., 2020), and left-right asymmetry in the density of presynaptic sites of protocerebral bridge to lateral accessory lobe-projecting neurons predicts an individual fly's idiosyncratic turning bias (Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Left-right asymmetry in the density of presynaptic sites of protocerebral bridge to lateral accessory lobe-projecting neurons predicts an individual fly's idiosyncratic turning bias.
source: Wiring asymmetry in an individual fly's dorsal cluster neurons is predictive of the straightness of its object-oriented walking behavior (Linneweber et al., 2020), and left-right asymmetry in the density of presynaptic sites of protocerebral bridge to lateral accessory lobe-projecting neurons predicts an individual fly's idiosyncratic turning bias (Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The number of synaptic connections from the pC2l to pIP10 neurons correlates with male song rate during courtship.
source: The number of synaptic connections from the pC2l to pIP10 neurons correlates with male song rate during courtship (Lillvis et al., 2022), and the presence of ectopic branches in neurons of the T2 hemilineage predicts delayed spontaneous flight initiation (Mellert et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The presence of ectopic branches in neurons of the T2 hemilineage predicts delayed spontaneous flight initiation.
source: The number of synaptic connections from the pC2l to pIP10 neurons correlates with male song rate during courtship (Lillvis et al., 2022), and the presence of ectopic branches in neurons of the T2 hemilineage predicts delayed spontaneous flight initiation (Mellert et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Individual odor preferences are stable over timescales longer than the experiment.
source: Individual odor preferences are stable over timescales longer than this experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E showing preference persistence over 3 and 24 hours.

claim: ORN and PN odor responses were roughly stereotyped across individuals.
source: Both ORN and PN odor responses were roughly stereotyped across individuals (Figure 1G and H), but also idiosyncratic (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1G and H and a citation to a previous study.

claim: ORN and PN odor responses were idiosyncratic.
source: Both ORN and PN odor responses were roughly stereotyped across individuals (Figure 1G and H), but also idiosyncratic (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1G and H and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Responses in PNs appeared to be more idiosyncratic than ORNs.
source: Responses in PNs appeared to be more idiosyncratic than ORNs (Figure 1J); a logistic linear classifier decoding fly identity from glomerular responses was more accurate when trained on PN than ORN responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: A logistic linear classifier decoding fly identity from glomerular responses was more accurate when trained on PN than ORN responses.
source: Responses in PNs appeared to be more idiosyncratic than ORNs (Figure 1J); a logistic linear classifier decoding fly identity from glomerular responses was more accurate when trained on PN than ORN responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: PN responses were more variable within flies, as measured across the left and right hemisphere ALs, compared to ORN responses.
source: PN responses were more variable within flies, as measured across the left and right hemisphere ALs, compared to ORN responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 6C; p<2 × 10–5, Mann–Whitney U test), suggesting that odor representations become more divergent farther from the sensory periphery.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 6C and a statistical test.

claim: No PCs of ORN neural activity could linearly predict OCT-MCH preference beyond the level of shuffled controls.
source: No PCs of ORN neural activity could linearly predict OCT-MCH preference beyond the level of shuffled controls (n = 35 flies) (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1K and L.

claim: The best ORN PC model only predicted odor-vs.-odor behavior with a nominal R2 of 0.031.
source: The best ORN PC model only predicted odor-vs.-odor behavior with a nominal R2 of 0.031.
evidence: This statement is supported by the statistical analysis of the ORN calcium data.

claim: PC 2 of PN activity was a statistically significant predictor of odor preference, accounting for 15% of preference variance in a training set of 47 flies (p=0.0063).
source: In contrast, PC 2 of PN activity was a statistically significant predictor of odor preference, accounting for 15% of preference variance in a training set of 47 flies (p=0.0063; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and 31% of preference variance on test data of flies (p=0.0069; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: PC 2 of PN activity accounted for 31% of preference variance on test data of flies (p=0.0069).
source: In contrast, PC 2 of PN activity was a statistically significant predictor of odor preference, accounting for 15% of preference variance in a training set of 47 flies (p=0.0063; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and 31% of preference variance on test data of flies (p=0.0069; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and statistical analysis.

claim: Combined train/test statistics for PN PC2 predicting OCT-MCH preference are R2 = 0.20; p=0.0001.
source: Combined train/test statistics (R2 = 0.20; p=0.0001) are presented in Figure 1K and M.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1K and M and statistical analysis.

claim: Idiosyncratic PN calcium predicts odor vs. odor preference.
source: Thus, idiosyncratic PN calcium predicts odor vs. odor preference.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of PN calcium responses and behavior.

claim: The measured correlation between calcium and behavior (R2latent) would be 0.46 in the absence of sampling error and temporal instability.
source: This analysis suggests that the measured correlation between calcium and behavior (R2latent) would be 0.46 in the absence of sampling error and temporal instability, but the uncertainty in this estimate is high (90% CI 0.06–0.90).
evidence: This statement is supported by the statistical inference analysis described in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: PC 1 of ORN calcium responses explained 23% of OCT-AIR preference variance (n = 30 flies, p=0.0099).
source: We found a suggestive correlate: PC 1 of ORN calcium responses explained 23% of preference variance (n = 30 flies, p=0.0099, Figure 1—figure supplement 10B), but this association was dominated by a single outlier (R2 of 0.078, p=0.14 with the outlier removed).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 10B and statistical analysis.

claim: The association between PC 1 of ORN calcium responses and OCT-AIR preference was dominated by a single outlier.
source: We found a suggestive correlate: PC 1 of ORN calcium responses explained 23% of preference variance (n = 30 flies, p=0.0099, Figure 1—figure supplement 10B), but this association was dominated by a single outlier (R2 of 0.078, p=0.14 with the outlier removed).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data with and without the outlier.

claim: Variation across individuals was correlated at the level of glomeruli much more strongly than odorant.
source: The loadings of the ORN and PN PCs indicate that variation across individuals was correlated at the level of glomeruli much more strongly than odorant (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 8).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 8.

claim: Stochastic variation in the olfactory circuit results in individual-level fluctuations in the responses of glomeruli-specific rather than odor-specific responses.
source: This suggests that stochastic variation in the olfactory circuit results in individual-level fluctuations in the responses of glomeruli-specific rather than odor-specific responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA loadings showing glomerulus-level organization.

claim: The loadings of PC2 of PN calcium responses contrast the responses of the DM2 and DC2 glomeruli with opposing weights.
source: In the odor-vs.-odor preference model, the loadings of PC2 of PN calcium responses contrast the responses of the DM2 and DC2 glomeruli with opposing weights (Figure 2A), suggesting that the activation of DM2 relative to DC2 predicts the likelihood of a fly preferring OCT to MCH.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The activation of DM2 relative to DC2 predicts the likelihood of a fly preferring OCT to MCH.
source: In the odor-vs.-odor preference model, the loadings of PC2 of PN calcium responses contrast the responses of the DM2 and DC2 glomeruli with opposing weights (Figure 2A), suggesting that the activation of DM2 relative to DC2 predicts the likelihood of a fly preferring OCT to MCH.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA loadings and supported by the linear model in Figure 2C.

claim: A linear model constructed from the average DM2 minus average DC2 PN response showed a statistically significant correlation with preference for OCT vs. MCH (R2 = 0.12; p=0.0035).
source: Indeed, a linear model constructed from the average DM2 minus average DC2 PN response (Figure 2B) showed a statistically significant correlation with preference for OCT vs. MCH (R2 = 0.12; p=0.0035; Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2B and 2C and statistical analysis.

claim: Greater activation of DM2 vs. DC2 correlates with preference for MCH.
source: The model slope coefficient was negative (Table 1), indicating that greater activation of DM2 vs. DC2 correlates with preference for MCH.
evidence: This statement is supported by the model coefficient in Table 1.

claim: The relative responses of DM2 vs. DC2 in PNs compactly predict an individual's preference for OCT vs. MCH.
source: With respect to odor-vs.-odor behavior, we conclude that the relative responses of DM2 vs. DC2 in PNs compactly predict an individual's preference.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DM2-DC2 model results.

claim: Applying the PN PC 2 model to yoked calcium responses did not predict flies' odor experience (R2 = 0.019, p=0.49).
source: Applying the PN PC 2 model to the yoked calcium responses did not predict flies' odor experience (R2 = 0.019, p=0.49; Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2E and statistical analysis.

claim: PN calcium responses predict odor preference rather than odor experience.
source: This is consistent with PN calcium responses predicting odor preference rather than odor experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the yoked control experiment results.

claim: In all cases, behavior prediction rose during odor delivery when applying calcium-to-behavior models to time-varying calcium signals.
source: Applying our calcium-to-behavior models (PN PC2-odor-vs.-odor, as well as ORN PC1-odor-vs.-air, PN PC1-odor-vs.-air) to the time-varying calcium signals, we found that in all cases behavior prediction rose during odor delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In ORNs, the predictive accuracy of behavior from calcium remained high after odor offset, whereas in PNs it declined.
source: In ORNs, the predictive accuracy remained high after odor offset, whereas in PNs it declined.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The times during which calcium responses predicted individual behavior generally aligned to the times during which a linear classifier could decode odor identity from neuronal responses.
source: The times during which calcium responses predicted individual behavior generally aligned to the times during which a linear classifier could decode odor identity from neuronal responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that idiosyncrasies in odor encoding predict individual preferences.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Idiosyncrasies in odor encoding predict individual preferences.
source: The times during which calcium responses predicted individual behavior generally aligned to the times during which a linear classifier could decode odor identity from neuronal responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that idiosyncrasies in odor encoding predict individual preferences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal alignment of behavior prediction and odor decoding.

claim: Brp-Short density was consistent across hemispheres.
source: This measure was consistent across hemispheres (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), while also showing variation among individuals, like calcium responses.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Brp-Short density showed variation among individuals.
source: This measure was consistent across hemispheres (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), while also showing variation among individuals, like calcium responses.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PC 2 of Brp-Short density was the best predictor of odor-vs.-odor preferences in training data (R2 = 0.22, n = 22 flies, p=0.028).
source: As in the PN calcium response models, PC 2 of Brp-Short density was the best predictor of odor-vs.-odor preferences in training data (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I, R2 = 0.22, n = 22 flies, p=0.028) and for test data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, R2 = 0.078, n = 31 flies, p=0.13; statistics from combined train and test data: R2 = 0.088, n = 53 flies, p=0.031; Figure 3F; median R2latent 0.15, 90% CI 0.00–0.74).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3D, E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and statistical analysis.

claim: PC 2 of Brp-Short density predicted odor-vs.-odor preferences in test data (R2 = 0.078, n = 31 flies, p=0.13).
source: As in the PN calcium response models, PC 2 of Brp-Short density was the best predictor of odor-vs.-odor preferences in training data (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I, R2 = 0.22, n = 22 flies, p=0.028) and for test data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, R2 = 0.078, n = 31 flies, p=0.13; statistics from combined train and test data: R2 = 0.088, n = 53 flies, p=0.031; Figure 3F; median R2latent 0.15, 90% CI 0.00–0.74).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and statistical analysis.

claim: Combined train and test data for Brp-Short density predicting OCT-MCH preference: R2 = 0.088, n = 53 flies, p=0.031.
source: As in the PN calcium response models, PC 2 of Brp-Short density was the best predictor of odor-vs.-odor preferences in training data (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I, R2 = 0.22, n = 22 flies, p=0.028) and for test data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, R2 = 0.078, n = 31 flies, p=0.13; statistics from combined train and test data: R2 = 0.088, n = 53 flies, p=0.031; Figure 3F; median R2latent 0.15, 90% CI 0.00–0.74).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3F and statistical analysis.

claim: The best presynaptic density models are less predictive of behavior than the best calcium response models (R2 = 0.088 vs. R2 = 0.22).
source: The best presynaptic density models are less predictive of behavior than the best calcium response models (R2 = 0.088 vs. R2 = 0.22; R2latent 0.15 and 0.46, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D vs. Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and J), suggesting that presynaptic density variation is not the full explanation of calcium response variability.
evidence: This statement is supported by comparing the R2 values from the Brp-Short and calcium models.

claim: Presynaptic density variation is not the full explanation of calcium response variability.
source: The best presynaptic density models are less predictive of behavior than the best calcium response models (R2 = 0.088 vs. R2 = 0.22; R2latent 0.15 and 0.46, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D vs. Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and J), suggesting that presynaptic density variation is not the full explanation of calcium response variability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the predictive power of Brp-Short and calcium models.

claim: Differences in presynaptic inputs to PNs may contribute to variation in the calcium dynamics of those neurons, in turn giving rise to individual preferences for OCT vs. MCH.
source: Nevertheless, differences in presynaptic inputs to PNs may contribute to variation in the calcium dynamics of those neurons, in turn giving rise to individual preferences for OCT vs. MCH.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Brp-Short and calcium results.

claim: The simulated AL recapitulated four canonical properties seen experimentally: typical firing rates at baseline and during odor stimulation, a more uniform distribution of PN firing rates compared to ORN rates, greater separation of PN odor representations compared to ORN representations, and a sublinear transfer function between ORNs and PNs.
source: We explored this parameter space manually and identified a configuration in which AL simulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) recapitulated four canonical properties seen experimentally (Figure 4—figure supplement 2): (1) typical firing rates at baseline and during odor stimulation (Bhandawat et al., 2007; Dubin and Harris, 1997; Jeanne and Wilson, 2015; Seki et al., 2010), (2) a more uniform distribution of PN firing rates compared to ORN rates (Bhandawat et al., 2007), (3) greater separation of PN odor representations compared to ORN representations (Bhandawat et al., 2007), and (4) a sublinear transfer function between ORNs and PNs (Bhandawat et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citations to published studies.

claim: Variation in PN responses due solely to Poisson timing of ORN input spikes was not organized at the glomerular level.
source: As a negative control, variation in PN responses due solely to Poisson timing of ORN input spikes (i.e., absent any circuit idiosyncrasy) was not organized at the glomerular level (Figure 4H).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: Resampling PN input-synapse density across glomeruli produced PN response correlations strongly organized by glomerulus.
source: As a positive control that the model can recapitulate this empirical structure, we resampled PN input-synapse density across glomeruli, producing PN response correlations strongly organized by glomerulus (Figure 4I).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4I.

claim: Bootstrapping ORN population compositions yielded a strong glomerular organization in PN responses.
source: Strikingly, bootstrapping ORN population compositions yielded a strong glomerular organization in PN responses (Figure 4J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: The loadings of the top PCs under ORN bootstrapping are dominated by responses of a single glomerulus to all odors, including DM2 and DC2.
source: The loadings of the top PCs under ORN bootstrapping are dominated by responses of a single glomerulus to all odors, including DM2 and DC2.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: Bootstrapping LNs produced much less glomerular organization in PN responses.
source: Bootstrapping LNs, in contrast, produced much less glomerular organization (Figure 4K), with little resemblance to the loadings of the empirical calcium PCs.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4K.

claim: DM2 and DC2 stand out in the PCA loadings under PN input-synapse density resampling and ORN bootstrapping.
source: DM2 and DC2 (also DL5) stand out in the PCA loadings under PN input-synapse density resampling and ORN bootstrapping (Figure 4I and J), suggesting that behaviorally-relevant PN coding variation is recapitulated in this modeling framework.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4I and J.

claim: High accuracy in distinguishing OCT- vs. MCH-preferring ALs was attained under PN input-synapse density resampling and ORN bootstrapping.
source: High accuracy was attained under PN input-synapse density resampling and ORN bootstrapping (sources of circuit variation that produced PN response loadings highlighting DM2 and DC2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Developmental variability in ORN populations may drive patterns of PN physiological variation that in turn drive individuality in odor-vs.-odor choice behavior.
source: Thus, developmental variability in ORN populations may drive patterns of PN physiological variation that in turn drive individuality in odor-vs.-odor choice behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results showing that ORN bootstrapping recapitulates empirical PN response patterns.

claim: The difference in the activation of PNs in DC2 and DM2 during odor exposure predicts idiosyncratic OCT-vs.-MCH preferences.
source: Specifically, the difference in the activation of PNs in DC2 and DM2 during odor exposure predicts idiosyncratic OCT-vs.-MCH preferences (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the calcium imaging experiments.

claim: This circuit element is in the olfactory sensory periphery and explains a large portion of the individuality signal.
source: This circuit element is in the olfactory sensory periphery and explains a large portion of the individuality signal, suggesting that behavioral idiosyncrasy arises early and suddenly in the sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the location of the identified locus of individuality and the strength of the correlation.

claim: Behavioral idiosyncrasy arises early and suddenly in the sensorimotor transformation.
source: This circuit element is in the olfactory sensory periphery and explains a large portion of the individuality signal, suggesting that behavioral idiosyncrasy arises early and suddenly in the sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the location of the identified locus of individuality.

claim: Loci of individuality are likely to vary, even within the sensory periphery, with the specific behavioral paradigm (i.e., odor-vs.-odor or odor-vs.-air).
source: Another key conclusion is that loci of individuality are likely to vary, even within the sensory periphery, with the specific behavioral paradigm (i.e., odor-vs.-odor or odor-vs.-air).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the different neural correlates found for odor-vs.-odor and odor-vs.-air behaviors.

claim: Low persistence of odor preference may be attributable to factors like internal states or plasticity.
source: Low persistence of odor preference may be attributable to factors like internal states or plasticity.
evidence: This is speculation about the causes of low behavioral persistence.

claim: Brp glomerular density was a significant predictor of individual odor-vs.-odor preferences.
source: Brp glomerular density was a significant predictor of individual odor-vs.-odor preferences (Figure 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The strongest predictor of OCT-MCH preference among principal components of Brp-Short density features contrastive loadings between DM2 and other glomeruli, similar to the DM2-DC2 contrast present in the model that predicts odor preference from PN calcium.
source: The strongest predictor of OCT-MCH preference among principal components of Brp-Short density features contrastive loadings between DM2 and other glomeruli, similar to the DM2-DC2 contrast present in the model that predicts odor preference from PN calcium.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: The predictive relationship between Brp and behavior was weaker than that of PN calcium responses.
source: The predictive relationship between Brp and behavior was weaker than that of PN calcium responses, suggesting there are other determinants, such as other synaptic proteins, neurite morphology, or the influence of idiosyncratic LNs (Chou et al., 2010) modulating the ORN-PN transformation (Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the R2 values of Brp-Short and calcium models.

claim: There are other determinants of PN calcium response variability besides Brp density, such as other synaptic proteins, neurite morphology, or the influence of idiosyncratic LNs.
source: The predictive relationship between Brp and behavior was weaker than that of PN calcium responses, suggesting there are other determinants, such as other synaptic proteins, neurite morphology, or the influence of idiosyncratic LNs (Chou et al., 2010) modulating the ORN-PN transformation (Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about other possible determinants of PN calcium variability, with citations to relevant studies.

claim: The model recapitulated canonical AL computations.
source: With light parameter tuning, this model recapitulated canonical AL computations, providing a baseline for assessing the effects of idiosyncratic stochastic variation.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The apparent variation in odor responses across simulated individuals is less than that seen in the empirical calcium responses.
source: The apparent variation in odor responses across simulated individuals (Figure 4F) is less than that seen in the empirical calcium responses (Figure 1H), likely due to (1) biological phenomena missing from the model, (2) the lack of measurement noise, and (3) the fact that our perturbations are applied to the connectome of a single fly.
evidence: This is an observation comparing simulated and empirical data, with speculation about the causes.

claim: Simulating idiosyncratic ALs by varying PN input synapse density or bootstrapping ORNs produced correlated PN responses across odors in DC2 and DM2, matching experimental results.
source: When examining PCA loadings, however, simulating idiosyncratic ALs by varying PN input synapse density or bootstrapping ORNs produced correlated PN responses across odors in DC2 and DM2, matching our experimental results.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in Figure 4I and J.

claim: These sources of variation specifically implicate the ORN-PN synapse as an important substrate for establishing behaviorally relevant patterns of PN response variation.
source: These sources of variation specifically implicate the ORN-PN synapse (like our Brp results) as an important substrate for establishing behaviorally relevant patterns of PN response variation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results showing that ORN-PN synapse variation recapitulates empirical patterns.

claim: The flies used in the experiments were isogenic and reared in standardized laboratory conditions that produce reduced behavioral individuality compared to enriched environments.
source: The flies used in our experiments were isogenic and reared in standardized laboratory conditions that produce reduced behavioral individuality compared to enriched environments (Akhund-Zade et al., 2019; Körholz et al., 2018; Zocher et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement describes the experimental conditions and is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Even standardized laboratory conditions yield substantial behavioral individuality.
source: Yet, even these conditions yield substantial behavioral individuality.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Variability in the expression of the flies' transgenes is not expected to be a major driver of behavioral individuality.
source: We do not expect variability in the expression of the flies' transgenes to be a major driver of this individuality as wildtype flies have a similarly broad distribution of odor preferences (Honegger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study showing similar individuality in wildtype flies.

claim: Behavioral variation may be beneficial, supporting a bet-hedging strategy to counter environmental fluctuations.
source: Behavioral variation may be beneficial, supporting a bet-hedging strategy (Hopper, 1999) to counter environmental fluctuations (Akhund-Zade et al., 2020; Honegger et al., 2020; Kain et al., 2015; Krams et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation about the adaptive value of behavioral variation, supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: PN response variation appears to be partially rooted in glomerular Brp variation.
source: Just as PN response variation appears to be partially rooted in glomerular Brp variation, the latter has its own causal roots, including, perhaps, stochasticity in gene expression (Li et al., 2017; Raj et al., 2010), itself a predictor of idiosyncratic behavioral biases (Werkhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Brp and calcium results, with speculation about deeper causal roots supported by citations.

claim: Stochasticity in gene expression is a predictor of idiosyncratic behavioral biases.
source: Just as PN response variation appears to be partially rooted in glomerular Brp variation, the latter has its own causal roots, including, perhaps, stochasticity in gene expression (Li et al., 2017; Raj et al., 2010), itself a predictor of idiosyncratic behavioral biases (Werkhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.
